blocks.text: Quick verdict

Bright Data is the better choice for scraping and data collection at scale, especially on hardened targets, where its pool depth, targeting precision and managed unblocking products save engineering time. NodeMaven is the better choice for social media, multi-accounting and anti-detect browser work: its pre-screened IPs, long sticky sessions, rollover and cashback protect accounts, and it is cheaper at small volumes ($45 for 10 GB against $80 at Bright Data's list price) and at 100 GB (about $220 against a $499 minimum plan).

Bright Data and NodeMaven both charge more than budget providers and both emphasise quality, but in different ways. Bright Data offers the broadest web-data platform, with a 150M+ pool, carrier, ZIP and ASN targeting, and managed Web Unlocker, SERP API and Scraping Browser products. NodeMaven focuses narrowly on IP cleanliness, screening each residential and mobile IP before assignment for account-based work. This comparison helps you decide which kind of quality you need.

blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
NodeMaven in 2026: what you get

NodeMaven is the quality-first option. Instead of handing out whatever IP the pool returns, it screens addresses in real time and lets you choose how strict the screening is. That matters most for account-based work such as social media management and multi-accounting, where a flagged IP can cost you an account. The price reflects it: $4.50/GB without a plan and $2.20/GB on monthly plans.

Strengths: IP Quality Filter screens IPs before you get them; Long sticky sessions for account work; Traffic rollover and cashback; Quality guarantee that pays for bad IPs. Weak spots: Smaller pool than mass-market networks; No datacenter proxies; Pay-as-you-go rate is double the plan rate.
Pricing: Bright Data vs NodeMaven

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

NodeMaven charges $4.50/GB pay-as-you-go and $2.20/GB on monthly plans, with residential and mobile traffic on one balance. A $3.50 trial includes 750 MB. Unused traffic rolls over, and you earn up to 10% cashback on used traffic. ISP proxies start at $2.99 per IP with unlimited traffic.

For a 10 GB month, NodeMaven costs about $45 while Bright Data costs about $80, so NodeMaven saves around 44%. At 100 GB a month, NodeMaven is the cheaper option at about $220 against $499 for Bright Data, roughly 56% less. Look past the per-GB figure too. NodeMaven lets unused traffic carry forward, while Bright Data's allowance does not (monthly plan allowances reset each cycle). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, Bright Data (150M+) is about 5.0x larger than NodeMaven (30M+ residential + 250K mobile). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and NodeMaven lists 150+. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while NodeMaven offers country, region, city and ISP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and NodeMaven offers rotating or long sticky sessions (multi-day). Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. The limitation on the NodeMaven side: the quality filter matters less for high-rotation crawling.

SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. How NodeMaven compares: workable, but you pay a premium for filtering you may not need.

Social media and multi-account management: NodeMaven. NodeMaven has the edge here. Why: pre-screened, low-fraud-score IPs with long sticky sessions. How Bright Data compares: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. How NodeMaven compares: fine for light checks.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. How NodeMaven compares: good quality but a smaller pool.
Tight budgets: NodeMaven wins. The deciding factor for NodeMaven: mid-priced on plans, expensive on PAYG. The limitation on the Bright Data side: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. NodeMaven: Standard. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and NodeMaven before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Bright Data and NodeMaven is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.

3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country. 4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, NodeMaven in 2, and 0 are ties. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while NodeMaven is strongest for social media and multi-account management. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
